$comment: Knowledge points for cl_foundations. Each topic's knowledge points are ordered: the first covers the most basic idea, later ones introduce harder cases. Mastery of a topic = clearing every knowledge point in order. `keyPrerequisites` name the topics a targeted remedial review draws from when a learner fails the same knowledge point twice.

knowledgePoints.name: The four steps that disappear
knowledgePoints.teach:
In Building with the Claude API the agentic loop is yours, and it is always the same four steps:

while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(...)          # 1. call
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use": break     # 2. inspect stop_reason
    result = run_tool(resp.content[-1])          # 3. dispatch the tool yourself
    messages.append(tool_result_block(result))   # 4. append and go around again

The Agent SDK runs that loop for you and hands you a stream of messages instead. All four steps vanish from your code.

What replaces them is not nothing. What you own shifts from mechanism — how the loop turns — to policy: which tools exist, who may call them, when to stop, and what runs around each call. Every option you will meet in this section is a policy knob.

questions.q: You port a working hand-rolled agent to the Agent SDK. Which of your code disappears entirely?
options: The tool implementations — the SDK ships its own versions
The stop_reason check, the tool dispatch, the tool_result append, and the re-call
The system prompt and the model choice
Retry and backoff, which the SDK handles at the HTTP layer
questions.explain: The loop mechanism goes. Your tool implementations, prompt, and model choice all survive — they are policy, and policy is still yours.

questions.q: Which of these is a policy concern the SDK expects you to own, rather than mechanism it owns for you?
options: Appending tool_result blocks in the right order
Deciding which tools the agent is allowed to call
Detecting stop_reason == "tool_use"
Re-issuing the request after a tool runs
questions.explain: Three of these are turns of the crank. Which tools exist and who may call them is the decision the SDK deliberately leaves to you.

knowledgePoints.name: Why the delta matters for the exam
knowledgePoints.teach:
The hand-rolled loop is still tested. The SDK is the delta on top of it, not a replacement for knowing it.

A useful reading habit for exam questions: when a scenario describes something going wrong inside the loop — a tool never runs, a turn never ends, a result never comes back — ask whether the fix is a policy you failed to state, not a mechanism you failed to write. With the SDK, mechanism bugs are rarely yours.

questions.q: An SDK agent never calls a tool you know it has. Where do you look first?
options: The loop implementation, for a missing stop_reason branch
Policy: whether the tool is registered, allowed, and described well enough to be selected
The HTTP client, for a dropped tool_result block
The model's temperature setting
questions.explain: You no longer own the branch or the block. Registration, permission, and description are the three policy surfaces that can silently stop a tool from being used.

questions.q: Why does the Agent SDK section still assume you know the hand-rolled loop?
options: Because the SDK falls back to it when the subprocess is unavailable
Because the exam tests both, and SDK options are named after loop concepts like turns and tool results
Because you must implement the loop before the SDK will accept your tools
Because Python users must hand-roll while TypeScript users do not
questions.explain: maxTurns, tool_result, stop_reason — the vocabulary of the SDK's options is the vocabulary of the loop it absorbed.

reviewQuestions.q: What is the single sentence that describes what changes when you adopt the Agent SDK?
options: You trade a slower loop for a faster one
You stop owning mechanism and start owning policy
You gain streaming and lose tool use
You move from Python to TypeScript
reviewQuestions.explain: Mechanism → policy. Everything else in this section is a consequence of that trade.

knowledgePoints.name: One fact explains the whole surface area
knowledgePoints.teach:
Here is the fact that makes the rest of the SDK stop feeling arbitrary:

The SDK spawns the Claude Code CLI as a subprocess and talks to it over a control protocol.

It is a steering wheel bolted onto a car that already exists. Which is why a library — something you would expect to be a thin HTTP client — has permission modes, hooks, settings files, CLAUDE.md loading, and subagents. Those are Claude Code's features, exposed programmatically.

It also explains options that would be nonsense in an HTTP client: pathToClaudeCodeExecutable, spawnClaudeCodeProcess, and settingSources.

questions.q: Why does the Agent SDK have permission modes and settings files when the raw Messages API has neither?
options: They were added to match competitor feature lists
The SDK spawns the Claude Code CLI as a subprocess, so Claude Code's features come along with it
The Messages API exposes them on a beta header
MCP requires them in order to register tools
questions.explain: One fact, most of the API surface. Hold onto it — it lets you guess correctly about features you have not read the docs for yet.

questions.q: Which option is a direct tell that something other than an HTTP request is happening?
options: maxTokens
pathToClaudeCodeExecutable
temperature
systemPrompt
questions.explain: You do not point an HTTP client at an executable. That option only makes sense because there is a process being spawned.

knowledgePoints.name: Using the model to predict features
knowledgePoints.teach:
The model earns its keep as a prediction tool. If a capability exists in the Claude Code CLI, the default assumption is that it is reachable from the SDK — usually under a camelCase version of the same name.

Skills, memory, plugins, MCP servers, hooks, permission modes, CLAUDE.md, subagents in .claude/agents/: all of these are Claude Code concepts you will meet again as SDK options.

The converse is also useful. If something is not a Claude Code feature — say, prompt caching controls or a beta header — expect it to belong to the API layer instead, and not to appear as an SDK option at all.

questions.q: You have never read the subagents docs. Using the subprocess model, what do you predict about where subagent definitions can live?
options: Only in code, since a library cannot read files
In code and on disk under .claude/, because that is where Claude Code keeps them
Only in a hosted registry
Only in environment variables
questions.explain: That prediction is correct — programmatic definitions and .claude/agents/ markdown files, with the programmatic ones taking precedence.

questions.q: Which is the weakest reason to remember the subprocess model?
options: It predicts which features the SDK will have
It explains why disk settings affect an SDK app
It is the answer to a commonly asked exam question about why the SDK looks the way it does
It tells you which model version the SDK will use by default
questions.explain: Model selection has nothing to do with the subprocess. The other three are exactly what the model buys you.

reviewQuestions.q: State the mental model that explains permission modes, hooks, settings files, CLAUDE.md loading, and subagents in a client library.
options: The library re-implements each feature against the Messages API
The library spawns the Claude Code CLI as a subprocess and drives it over a control protocol
The features are part of the MCP specification
They are inherited from the Anthropic SDK clients
reviewQuestions.explain: The steering wheel and the car. Everything downstream follows from it.

knowledgePoints.name: Packages, calls, and options types
knowledgePoints.teach:
Two languages, same engine, different ignition keys:

TypeScriptPython
Package@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdkclaude-agent-sdk
One-off callquery({ prompt, options })query(prompt=..., options=...)
Options typeOptionsClaudeAgentOptions
ReturnsQuery — an AsyncGenerator with extra methodsAsyncIterator[Message]
Multi-turn client— (use query with resume)ClaudeSDKClient

The names are worth rote memorising. @anthropic-ai/claude-code is a different package; claude-sdk and @anthropic/agent-sdk are not packages at all.

questions.q: Which pair of package names is correct?
options: TypeScript @anthropic/agent-sdk · Python claude-sdk
TypeScript @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk · Python claude-agent-sdk
Both languages use claude-agent
TypeScript @anthropic-ai/claude-code · Python anthropic-agents
questions.explain: Same engine, two keys. And note the options types differ too: Options in TypeScript, ClaudeAgentOptions in Python.

questions.q: In Python, what does query() return?
options: A list of messages once the run completes
An AsyncIterator[Message] you consume as the run proceeds
A ClaudeSDKClient you then connect
A synchronous generator of strings
questions.explain: You iterate the stream. The TypeScript equivalent is a Query object, which is an AsyncGenerator with a few extra methods hung off it.

knowledgePoints.name: Pre-warming with startup()
knowledgePoints.teach:
Spawning a subprocess and completing an initialize handshake takes real time. If the first thing a user does is wait for it, they feel it.

startup() (TypeScript) pre-spawns the subprocess and finishes the handshake before a prompt exists, returning a WarmQuery. The first real query() then does not pay the spawn cost inline. The default initialize timeout is 60,000 ms.

This option only exists because of the subprocess. There is nothing to pre-warm in an HTTP client.

questions.q: What problem does startup() solve?
options: It caches the system prompt for cheaper tokens
It pays the subprocess spawn and handshake cost before the first prompt arrives
It validates your API key early
It preloads MCP tool schemas into the model's context
questions.explain: Latency, not cost or correctness. The default initialize timeout is 60,000 ms.

questions.q: Why is there no startup() equivalent in a plain HTTP client for the Messages API?
options: Because HTTP clients are always slower
Because there is no subprocess to spawn or handshake to complete
Because the Messages API does not support streaming
Because API keys are validated per request
questions.explain: Pre-warming is meaningful only because the SDK has a process to bring up first.

reviewQuestions.q: Which options type name goes with which language?
options: TypeScript ClaudeAgentOptions · Python Options
TypeScript Options · Python ClaudeAgentOptions
Both use AgentOptions
Both use ClaudeAgentOptions
reviewQuestions.explain: TypeScript keeps the bare name; Python spells it out. Worth drilling — it shows up as a distractor.

knowledgePoints.name: The comparison table
knowledgePoints.teach:
Featurequery()ClaudeSDKClient
SessionNew session by defaultReuses the same session
ConversationSingle exchangeMultiple exchanges, one context
ConnectionManaged automaticallyManual control
InterruptsNot supportedSupported
Continue chatManual via continue_conversation / resumeAutomatic
Use caseOne-off tasksContinuous conversations

Streaming input, hooks and custom tools work with both — those are not the discriminators.

questions.q: Which capability does query() simply not have?
options: Hooks
Custom in-process tools
Interrupts
Streaming input
questions.explain: Hooks, custom tools, and streaming input all work with either. Interrupts are the client's alone.

questions.q: How does query() behave with respect to sessions by default?
options: It reuses the most recent session automatically
It opens a new session on each call unless you pass resume or continue
It refuses to run twice without a session id
It shares one session per process
questions.explain: New session by default is the trap: an app that expected continuity and never passed resume gets an amnesiac agent.

knowledgePoints.name: The rule of thumb, applied
knowledgePoints.teach:
The rule worth memorising: if the next action depends on Claude's response, or you need to interrupt, use ClaudeSDKClient. Otherwise query().

Two worked cases:

  • Nightly job that summarises yesterday's tickets and writes a file. Nothing branches on the answer, nobody is watching, nothing to interrupt → query().
  • Support console where an operator watches the agent work and can cancel it. Interruption is a hard requirement → ClaudeSDKClient.

questions.q: A support console must let an operator cancel a long-running agent when the customer hangs up. Which entry point?
options: query(), with abortController
ClaudeSDKClient, because interrupts are only supported there
Either — interrupts work the same in both
query() with maxTurns set low
questions.explain: abortController and a low maxTurns both end a run, but neither is the interrupt facility the comparison table is pointing at. Interrupts belong to the client.

questions.q: A nightly batch job runs one prompt per ticket and writes results to disk. Which entry point, and why?
options: ClaudeSDKClient, so all tickets share context
query(), because each ticket is a one-off exchange with nothing branching on the reply
ClaudeSDKClient, because batch work always needs manual connection control
query(), because ClaudeSDKClient cannot use tools
questions.explain: Sharing context across unrelated tickets would be a bug, not a feature — it leaks one customer's details into another's run.

reviewQuestions.q: State the rule of thumb for choosing between query() and ClaudeSDKClient.
options: Use the client whenever you use tools
Use the client if the next action depends on Claude's response, or you need to interrupt
Use query() only in TypeScript
Use the client whenever you want streaming
reviewQuestions.explain: Dependence and interruption. Tools and streaming are available either way.

knowledgePoints.name: Minimal by default
knowledgePoints.teach:
This one trips people constantly. query() does not give you Claude Code's system prompt unless you ask for it.

  • Omit systemPrompt → a minimal prompt.
  • systemPrompt: "…" → your custom prompt, and only yours.
  • systemPrompt: { type: 'preset', preset: 'claude_code' } → Claude Code's full prompt.

So an SDK agent that feels dumber than the CLI on the same task usually is not misconfigured in any exotic way — it just never opted into the preset.

questions.q: You omit systemPrompt entirely. What does the agent get?
options: Claude Code's full system prompt, since the CLI is underneath
A minimal system prompt
No system prompt at all, which is an error
The prompt from CLAUDE.md
questions.explain: Minimal, not Claude Code's. Opting in is explicit precisely because most SDK apps are not coding agents.

questions.q: Your SDK agent behaves nothing like the Claude Code CLI on an identical coding task. What do you check first?
options: The model id
Whether systemPrompt opts into the claude_code preset
Whether hooks are blocking tools
The maxTurns value
questions.explain: Same engine, different instructions. The preset is the difference far more often than anything else.

knowledgePoints.name: append and excludeDynamicSections
knowledgePoints.teach:
Two modifiers sit on the preset form:

  • append: "…" — extends the preset rather than replacing it. This is how you add house rules without losing Claude Code's behaviour.
  • excludeDynamicSections: true — moves per-session context (the parts of the prompt that differ per machine and per run) into the first user message. The point is prompt-cache reuse: a prompt prefix that is identical across machines can be cached and shared; one that embeds today's working directory cannot.

questions.q: What is excludeDynamicSections: true for?
options: Shrinking the prompt to save tokens
Moving per-session context into the first user message so the cached prompt prefix is identical across machines
Removing tool definitions from the prompt
Disabling CLAUDE.md loading
questions.explain: It is a cache-hit optimisation. The dynamic content still reaches the model; it just stops poisoning the cacheable prefix.

questions.q: You want Claude Code's behaviour plus three company-specific rules. Which shape?
options: systemPrompt: "<your three rules>"
preset claude_code with append: "<your three rules>"
Omit systemPrompt and put the rules in CLAUDE.md only
Two queries, one per prompt
questions.explain: A bare string replaces the preset instead of extending it. append is the field that means "and also".

reviewQuestions.q: Which systemPrompt value gives an SDK agent Claude Code's full system prompt?
options: Omitting the field
{ type: 'preset', preset: 'claude_code' }
Any non-empty string
{ type: 'cli' }
reviewQuestions.explain: Explicit opt-in. Omitting gets you a minimal prompt; a string gets you only your own.

knowledgePoints.name: Three sources, three files
knowledgePoints.teach:
SettingSource = "user" | "project" | "local":

ValueFile
user~/.claude/settings.json
project.claude/settings.json (version controlled)
local.claude/settings.local.json (gitignored)
  • Omitted / undefined → loads all three, exactly like the CLI.
  • [] → disables user, project and local. Endpoint-managed policy still loads regardless.

questions.q: What does omitting settingSources do?
options: Disables all filesystem settings
Loads user, project, and local settings — the same as the CLI
Loads only project settings
Raises an error; the field is required
questions.explain: The default is CLI parity. You have to opt out, not opt in.

questions.q: You pass settingSources: []. What still loads?
options: Nothing at all
Endpoint-managed policy
User settings, because they are outside the project
Local settings, because they are gitignored
questions.explain: Organisation policy is not yours to switch off, and that is the point of it.

knowledgePoints.name: The CLAUDE.md bug, and the production default
knowledgePoints.teach:
The common bug: project CLAUDE.md loads only when "project" is in settingSources. An SDK app that ignores CLAUDE.md has almost always passed [], or a list that omitted "project".

Two gotchas worth carrying:

  • Python-only: in SDK 0.1.59 and earlier, setting_sources=[] behaved like omitting it, so it did not disable filesystem settings. TypeScript was never affected.
  • Production default: for a deployed product you usually want settingSources: [] — reproducible behaviour that does not change because a developer edited their personal settings file.

questions.q: An SDK app ignores the repo's CLAUDE.md. What is the most likely cause?
options: CLAUDE.md must be renamed for SDK use
settingSources was [] or a list without "project"
The systemPrompt preset was not set to claude_code
CLAUDE.md is only read by the CLI, never the SDK
questions.explain: "project" is what makes project CLAUDE.md load. This is the single most common settings bug in SDK apps.

questions.q: Why do deployed products usually pass settingSources: []?
options: It is faster, because no files are read
So behaviour is reproducible and cannot change because someone edited their personal settings
Because endpoint-managed policy requires it
Because CLAUDE.md is not allowed in production
questions.explain: Reproducibility. The cost is that you must then supply anything CLAUDE.md would have given you, explicitly.

reviewQuestions.q: Which settingSources value must be present for project CLAUDE.md to load?
options: "user"
"project"
"local"
Any of the three
reviewQuestions.explain: "project" specifically. Omitting the whole field also works, since that loads all three.

knowledgePoints.name: Guillotines vs. budgets the model can see
knowledgePoints.teach:
Four ways to stop a run, and they are not interchangeable:

  • maxTurns — maximum agentic turns (tool-use round trips). A guillotine: the run stops mid-thought when the count is hit.
  • maxBudgetUsd — stops when the client-side cost estimate reaches this figure. Also a guillotine.
  • taskBudget: { total } (alpha) — an API-side token budget, and the model is told its remaining budget so it can pace itself and wrap up deliberately.
  • abortController (TS) — cancellation from your side.

That third one is the distinctive fact. If a question asks which control lets the agent finish gracefully rather than be cut off, it is taskBudget.

questions.q: Which budget option does the model itself know about, so it can pace itself and wrap up?
options: maxTurns
maxBudgetUsd
taskBudget
abortController
questions.explain: maxTurns and maxBudgetUsd are guillotines. taskBudget is told to the model, which changes its behaviour rather than just ending it.

questions.q: maxBudgetUsd is enforced against what?
options: A server-side billing meter
A client-side cost estimate
The token budget the model is told about
Wall-clock time converted to dollars
questions.explain: Client-side estimate — which is why it is a safety rail rather than a billing guarantee.

knowledgePoints.name: Structured results
knowledgePoints.teach:
Stopping is half the problem; the other half is getting something your code can use.

outputFormat: { type: 'json_schema', schema } makes the agent's final result conform to a schema, so a caller can consume it without parsing prose. It pairs naturally with budgets: a run that must end at some point should end with something structured rather than a half-written paragraph.

questions.q: Your service needs the agent's final answer as an object with fixed fields. Which option?
options: outputFormat: { type: 'json_schema', schema }
systemPrompt with a JSON example appended
taskBudget with a low total
A PostToolUse hook that reformats the result
questions.explain: Prompting for JSON is the probabilistic version of this. outputFormat is the declared one.

questions.q: Which pairing makes the most sense for an unattended run that must always return something usable?
options: abortController plus free-text output
taskBudget plus outputFormat json_schema
maxTurns plus a longer system prompt
maxBudgetUsd plus streaming
questions.explain: The model paces itself against a budget it can see, and what it produces at the end has a shape your caller can rely on.

reviewQuestions.q: Rank these by how gracefully the run ends: maxTurns, taskBudget, abortController.
options: abortController is gentlest, then maxTurns, then taskBudget
taskBudget is gentlest because the model is told about it; maxTurns and abortController simply stop the run
All three are identical in effect
maxTurns is gentlest because turns are coarse
reviewQuestions.explain: Only taskBudget changes the model's behaviour before the limit is reached.
